opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as two sides of the same question: what is the next thing that is scarce?

For a long time the bottleneck was data and compute for pretraining. Then reasoning with reinforcement learning showed that if you have a reliable signal of right or wrong, the model can improve far beyond imitating human text. Math and competitive programming were natural first targets because verification is cheap. You check the answer, you run the tests.

ML coding is interesting because it is one step closer to the real thing. You're not solving a puzzle with a known answer. You're running experiments, reading logs, deciding what to try next, and the feedback is noisy and delayed. If a model can do good ML research engineering, it starts to feed back into its own development. Even partial progress there compounds. So I see ML coding less as an application and more as a testbed for whether models can do open-ended, empirical work.

Long horizon is the other half. Most current evaluations are short. Even hard reasoning problems are maybe minutes or an hour of human effort. Most valuable work takes days or weeks: keeping context, recovering from mistakes, knowing when you're stuck, deciding what matters. Today models are strong within a single attempt but fragile across many steps. Errors accumulate, and they don't yet have a good sense of their own progress.

My honest view is that the next paradigm shift probably won't come from just scaling the current recipe on longer tasks. Some things seem to be missing. One is memory, meaning real accumulation of experience rather than just a bigger context window. Another is learning from sparse, ambiguous rewards over long trajectories. A third is something like self-evaluation, where the model judges whether its own intermediate work is good. Humans do this all the time without an external grader.

So when I think about ML coding and long-horizon tasks, I don't see them as the paradigm itself. They're where the current paradigm visibly breaks, and that is exactly why they're valuable. If you want to find the next big idea, you look for the problems where more compute and more RL on verifiable tasks stop giving you clean gains. I think these two are right at that frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't see either of them as the next paradigm by themselves. They're more like the proving ground where the next paradigm will show up, if it shows up at all.

Let me explain what I mean. If you look at the history of the field, the big shifts weren't really about a new task. They were about a new source of scale. Pretraining was scale from internet text. Then RL on reasoning was scale from verifiable rewards, math and code, where you can check the answer cheaply. Each time, the community found a huge, cheap, reliable signal, and the models grew into it.

So the question I ask is, where is the next cheap, reliable signal? And I think both ML coding and long horizon tasks are interesting precisely because they stress the current recipe in ways it hasn't been stressed before.

ML coding is interesting to me for a slightly selfish reason, which is that it's the loop that produces more AI. If a model can genuinely do the work of a research engineer, set up an experiment, run it, read the result, decide what to try next, then the bottleneck on progress stops being the number of people at a lab. But what makes it hard is not the coding part. Models are already good at writing a training script. The hard part is that the feedback is slow and noisy. You launch a run, it takes hours, the loss curve is ambiguous, and you have to form a belief about what happened. That is not a verifiable reward in the way a math problem is. So ML coding forces you to confront the question of how a model learns from expensive, delayed, partially observed outcomes.

Long horizon is really the same question from the other side. The agent benchmarks we had a couple of years ago were mostly a few steps. You could get away with a model that was locally smart and had no real memory of what it was doing. Once you go to hundreds or thousands of actions, the failure mode changes completely. The model doesn't fail because it can't do step 50. It fails because by step 50 it has lost the thread of why it's there, or it's accumulated small errors that nobody corrected, or the context is full of garbage. Those are not problems you fix with a bigger model. They're problems about how an agent represents its own state over time, what it chooses to remember, how it recovers.

So when I put those two together, what I actually see is a gap in the recipe. We know how to do pretraining. We know how to do RL when the reward is clean. We don't really know how to do learning when experience is long, expensive, and the signal is diffuse. And I suspect that's where the next real change comes from. Not a new architecture, not another benchmark, but a way to turn messy long-horizon experience into training signal at scale. Whether that looks like better environments, or models that learn from their own trajectories more efficiently, or something about memory, I don't know yet.

What I'd push back on is the framing that a new paradigm has to look dramatically different from what we have. The reasoning models didn't look like a paradigm shift at first either. It was the same transformer, same pretraining, plus a relatively simple idea applied at scale. So I wouldn't be surprised if the next one also looks boring from the outside. The thing that would tell me it's real is if we start seeing models get meaningfully better at tasks that take days, with the same amount of compute, because they're learning from the process rather than just from the outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think ML coding and long-horizon tasks are two useful directions because they test different parts of what a next paradigm might require.

With ML coding, the interesting question is whether an AI can participate in the process of improving AI. Writing a training script is one piece, but you also need to propose an experiment, run it, interpret the results, and decide what to try next. If a system can do that reliably, it could accelerate research. That doesn’t automatically mean it will discover a new paradigm, but it could make the search much faster.

Long horizon asks whether the system can sustain that process. Can it work through many experiments, recover from failures, and revise its assumptions while keeping track of the original objective? A model can be very good at individual coding problems and still struggle with an open-ended research project. So there’s a gap between solving a step and managing the whole process.

The two directions meet when you ask an agent to pursue a research question over an extended period. That forces us to think about learning from interaction, evaluating intermediate progress, and allocating compute when the right answer isn’t known in advance.

I’d be cautious about calling either one the next paradigm by itself. They’re settings where we can discover what’s missing. The important signal would be a system that consistently turns more time and experimentation into better results, including on problems its designers don’t already know how to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ML coding and long-horizon tasks are two useful directions for exploring what the next paradigm might be, but I wouldn’t assume either one is already the answer.

With ML coding, the interesting possibility is that a model can participate in improving the learning system itself. It can write an experiment, run it, look at the results, and decide what to try next. But generating code is only one part of that. The harder question is whether it can consistently produce improvements that survive careful evaluation. If that loop works, you have a way to turn more computation into research progress.

Long horizon asks a related question: can an AI keep making useful progress over a much longer sequence of actions? A system might be very good at individual steps and still fail at a project because it loses track of the objective, makes an early mistake, or doesn’t know when to change direction. So extending the horizon involves memory, feedback, error recovery, and judgment about what to do next.

The two come together naturally in machine-learning research, because research is a long-horizon activity with some measurable feedback. You have to formulate a hypothesis, implement it, interpret an experiment, and sometimes realize that the hypothesis was wrong.

For me, the paradigm-level question is whether we can move from models that answer questions to systems that reliably carry out that whole learning process. ML coding gives us a concrete setting to test it, and long horizon describes a capability we need. Whether that requires a fundamentally new approach or emerges from improving the current approach is still an open question.
